========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, to be honest, I just... I really don't feel like myself anymore. I mean, I used to be able to at least get through the day and have a normal conversation, you know? But lately, I barely talk to people. I just go completely flat and quiet. It's like the volume gets turned all the way down inside my head and I can't find the dial to turn it back up. 

I work as a building cleaner, doing the evening shifts mostly, and usually, it's just me and my supplies. But lately... just getting started on the cleaning route feels like pushing a loaded cart uphill in the mud. I'll just stand there in the janitor's closet, looking at the mop bucket and the industrial cleaner, and I can't even muster the energy to mix it with the water. It’s this heaviness. And when someone does walk by, like one of the late-night office workers, I used to say hello, ask about their evening, maybe talk about the news or something—I took some college classes back in the day, so I always liked to keep up with things and chat. But now? I just stare. I don't have the words. I just feel so incredibly empty and flat, like all the air has been let out of my tires. 

It takes absolutely everything out of me just to put one foot in front of the other down those long, empty hallways. The whole night just stretches out in front of me, and I can't bring myself to care or to speak or to even move half the time. So, I guess that's why I'm here. Because pushing that heavy cart uphill every single night when I feel this hollowed out... it's just getting to be too much to handle on my own.

Well... no. No, I really don't. And that's... that's part of what makes it all so incredibly heavy, you know? Because I used to have things that I looked forward to. I wasn't just a guy pushing a mop. I had my little routines that brought me some peace. Like... Saturdays. Saturdays used to be my day. I'd wake up early, before the sun was even fully up, and I'd head down to the lake with my tackle box. I've been fishing since I was a boy—my grandfather taught me how to tie a proper knot when I was maybe seven or eight—and there was just something so... so calming about watching the water, feeling the line, waiting for that little tug. I didn't even care if I caught anything half the time, it was just the ritual of it. 

And then, on Sunday mornings, it was the crossword puzzle. I'd make a pot of strong coffee, sit at my little kitchen table—the one I had in my old apartment, right by the window where the morning light came in—and I'd work through the Sunday paper. I always did it in pen, too, which I was pretty proud of. And even at work, I used to get a kick out of showing the younger guys the ropes. You know, these kids come in, they think they know everything, but they don't know the first thing about properly stripping and waxing a linoleum floor without leaving streaks. I used to actually enjoy taking them aside, showing them the right technique, the right pressure to apply. It felt good to pass that on.

But now? Now... I don't know. The fishing rods are just gathering dust in the corner of my new place. I look at them, and I just think about the effort it would take to load the car, drive to the lake, bait the hook... and for what? I don't feel that calm anymore. I don't feel anything. The crossword puzzles just look like a jumble of meaningless boxes, and the coffee just tastes bitter. And at work, when a new guy comes on shift, I just let him make a mess of the floors. I don't say a word. I just watch him struggle, and I don't even care enough to step in. I just let all those things sit there—the fishing, the puzzles, the teaching—because I try to do them, or I think about doing them, and they just... they don't give me anything back anymore. It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in the bottom. You pour and you pour, but it just stays empty.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well... that’s... that’s a heavy question, isn't it? I guess... I mean, to be completely honest with you, and it's hard to say this, but... yes. Yes, I have. 

Now, I want to be clear right off the bat, I don't have some big plan. I'm not sitting in my apartment figuring out how to do something drastic, I'm not hoarding pills or anything like that. I've always been a practical guy, and honestly, like I said before, I barely have the energy to mix floor cleaner these days, let alone plan out something like ending it all. 

But... it’s the mornings. Well, my mornings, anyway, since I work the evening shift. I wake up in that new bedroom—the one where the window just faces a dirty brick wall instead of the street like my old place, where I used to be able to watch the neighborhood wake up—and I hear my alarm buzzing. And I just lie there staring at the ceiling. And a lot of mornings... a lot of mornings I wake up thinking it might just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. If I could have just slipped away in my sleep and stayed in the dark where it's quiet, where I don't have to face the empty hallways or the heavy cart or just... the sheer effort of existing for another twenty-four hours. Just the thought of having to put my feet on the floor feels impossible, like I'm wearing lead boots.

And I'll tell you, having that thought... realizing that I genuinely wouldn't mind if my life just quietly stopped... it scares me. It really does. It scares me enough to actually say it out loud to you right now, which isn't something I ever thought I'd do. You know, a man my age, you're supposed to just push through, have some grit, keep your chin up. My grandfather, the one who taught me to fish, he used to say you just put your head down and do the work. But when that first thought hits you before you've even thrown off the blankets, just wishing the world would go away permanently... it's terrifying. It really is. Because it happens so often now, just lying there, listening to the neighbor's TV through the thin walls, wishing I just wasn't here anymore.

Restless? No... no, I wouldn't say that. If anything, it’s, well, it's the exact opposite of that. I don't have any of that nervous energy, you know? You see some folks, maybe some of the guys I work with in the maintenance crew, they drink three or four cups of that terrible breakroom coffee and they're tapping their feet, pacing around the supply closet, just can't stay in one spot for two minutes. I was always on the move back then. But now, I just feel glued to the floor. Sitting still is just about the only thing I *can* do without it feeling like a monumental chore. Honestly, I could probably sit still all day if nobody made me get up.

Well, you know, it's funny you should ask that, because I was just noticing something about my uniform the other day. I've been wearing the same style of work pants for... oh, it's got to be fifteen years now. Dickies, navy blue, the ones with the reinforced knees because of all the bending and kneeling you have to do when you're scrubbing baseboards or fixing a leaky trap under a sink. Anyway, I always buy them a little snug around the waist because they stretch out, but lately... lately I've had to pull my belt in by at least two notches. Maybe three. They're just hanging off me, really. 

And it's not because I'm trying to lose weight or anything like that. I've never been one for diets or counting calories or whatever it is folks do. It's just... I don't know, my appetite is just gone. Completely gone. I'll open the fridge when I get home from my shift—usually around midnight, when the building is finally quiet and the last of the office workers have gone home—and I'll just stare at the shelves. I used to make myself a decent sandwich, maybe some turkey and Swiss on rye with a little bit of mustard, maybe heat up some soup if it was cold out. I always liked a good bowl of split pea soup. But now? Most days, food just tastes like cardboard. There's no flavor, no enjoyment in it whatsoever. It's just another chore, like everything else.

So a lot of times, I just skip meals altogether. I'll go the whole day on just that bitter coffee I mentioned, maybe a glass of water. Or if my stomach starts really gnawing at me, I'll just grab a handful of saltine crackers from the pantry and eat those standing over the sink before I go to bed. Just enough to stop the rumbling so I can try to get some sleep. But an actual, proper meal? Sitting down with a plate of hot food? I can't even remember the last time I had the desire to do that. It's just too much effort for something that brings me no satisfaction anyway. So, yeah, I'd say I've definitely lost some weight. I don't own a scale, but the way those work pants are fitting, it's pretty obvious.

Well, yes, that’s exactly it. That’s actually a big part of what brought me in here to talk to you in the first place, because I just don’t feel like myself anymore. Getting started on anything... it’s just a monumental task. 

Take my job, for instance. Getting started on my cleaning route every evening, it literally feels like I’m pushing a loaded cart uphill. And I mean a really loaded cart. You know those big grey utility carts we use? The ones with the heavy-duty casters? Normally you've got your mop bucket, your wringer, the yellow wet floor signs, all the industrial spray bottles hanging off the sides, maybe three or four heavy bags of wet trash. It's a heavy rig on a good day. But lately, just the thought of grabbing the handle of that cart and pushing it out of the basement supply closet... it feels like the wheels are locked and I'm trying to shove it up a steep hill in the mud. I'll just stand there in the closet with my hand on the plastic handle for... I don't know, ten, fifteen minutes sometimes, just trying to will my legs to take that very first step. Everything is just in slow motion. 

And it's not just the physical movement, either. It’s... I don't know how to explain it, but it's like my whole personality is in slow motion, too. I barely talk to people anymore. I just go completely flat and quiet. There’s this security guard, Frank, who works the front desk at the main building I clean. Good guy, maybe a few years older than me. We used to shoot the breeze every single night when I clocked in, talk about the baseball scores or how terrible the city traffic was getting, just normal everyday stuff. But now? Now I just kind of look at him. My face just feels... blank. Heavy. Like the muscles in my face just gave up and I can't even force a smile.

I've been fishing since I was a boy—my grandfather taught me how to tie a proper knot when I was maybe seven or eight—and there was just something so... so calming about watching the water, feeling the line, waiting for that little tug. I didn't even care if I caught anything half the time, it was just the ritual of it. \n\nAnd then, on Sunday mornings, it was the crossword puzzle. I'd make a pot of strong coffee, sit at my little kitchen table—the one I had in my old apartment, right by the window where the morning light came in—and I'd work through the Sunday paper. I always did it in pen, too, which I was pretty proud of. And even at work, I used to get a kick out of showing the younger guys the ropes. You know, these kids come in, they think they know everything, but they don't know the first thing about properly stripping and waxing a linoleum floor without leaving streaks. I used to actually enjoy taking them aside, showing them the right technique, the right pressure to apply. It felt good to pass that on.\n\nBut now? Now... I don't know. The fishing rods are just gathering dust in the corner of my new place. I look at them, and I just think about the effort it would take to load the car, drive to the lake, bait the hook... and for what? I don't feel that calm anymore. I don't feel anything. The crossword puzzles just look like a jumble of meaningless boxes, and the coffee just tastes bitter. And at work, when a new guy comes on shift, I just let him make a mess of the floors. I don't say a word. I just watch him struggle, and I don't even care enough to step in. I just let all those things sit there—the fishing, the puzzles, the teaching—because I try to do them, or I think about doing them, and they just... they don't give me anything back anymore. It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in the bottom. You pour and you pour, but it just stays empty.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about not wanting to live or had thoughts of suicide during this time?\n\nPatient: Well... that’s... that’s a heavy question, isn't it? I guess... I mean, to be completely honest with you, and it's hard to say this, but... yes. Yes, I have. \n\nNow, I want to be clear right off the bat, I don't have some big plan. I'm not sitting in my apartment figuring out how to do something drastic, I'm not hoarding pills or anything like that. I've always been a practical guy, and honestly, like I said before, I barely have the energy to mix floor cleaner these days, let alone plan out something like ending it all. \n\nBut... it’s the mornings. Well, my mornings, anyway, since I work the evening shift. I wake up in that new bedroom—the one where the window just faces a dirty brick wall instead of the street like my old place, where I used to be able to watch the neighborhood wake up—and I hear my alarm buzzing. And I just lie there staring at the ceiling. And a lot of mornings... a lot of mornings I wake up thinking it might just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. If I could have just slipped away in my sleep and stayed in the dark where it's quiet, where I don't have to face the empty hallways or the heavy cart or just... the sheer effort of existing for another twenty-four hours. Just the thought of having to put my feet on the floor feels impossible, like I'm wearing lead boots.\n\nAnd I'll tell you, having that thought... realizing that I genuinely wouldn't mind if my life just quietly stopped... it scares me. It really does. It scares me enough to actually say it out loud to you right now, which isn't something I ever thought I'd do. You know, a man my age, you're supposed to just push through, have some grit, keep your chin up. My grandfather, the one who taught me to fish, he used to say you just put your head down and do the work. But when that first thought hits you before you've even thrown off the blankets, just wishing the world would go away permanently... it's terrifying. It really is. Because it happens so often now, just lying there, listening to the neighbor's TV through the thin walls, wishing I just wasn't here anymore.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your movement or activity level, such as feeling restless or having trouble sitting still?\n\nPatient: Restless? No... no, I wouldn't say that. If anything, it’s, well, it's the exact opposite of that. I don't have any of that nervous energy, you know? You see some folks, maybe some of the guys I work with in the maintenance crew, they drink three or four cups of that terrible breakroom coffee and they're tapping their feet, pacing around the supply closet, just can't stay in one spot for two minutes. But me? I don't have that at all. Like I was saying before about the heaviness... it really settles into my bones. \n\nI have this old recliner in my new living room—it's this faded green corduroy thing I’ve had since maybe '98, dragged it all the way from the old apartment, which was a nightmare to get up the stairs here—and I can just sink into that chair and not move a muscle for hours. I don't even turn the television on most of the time. I just sit there. The thought of getting up, even just to walk the ten feet to the kitchen sink for a glass of tap water, it feels like I'd be trying to walk through wet cement. \n\nSo, no, pacing around or feeling antsy... that's not me. Even pushing the cart down the hallway at work, I used to have a pretty good clip to my step, especially back in my younger days when I was taking some night classes at the community college and always hustling from the bus stop to the campus and then to my shift. I was always on the move back then. But now, I just feel glued to the floor. Sitting still is just about the only thing I *can* do without it feeling like a monumental chore. Honestly, I could probably sit still all day if nobody made me get up.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost any weight over the past year and a half?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, it's funny you should ask that, because I was just noticing something about my uniform the other day. Anyway, I always buy them a little snug around the waist because they stretch out, but lately... lately I've had to pull my belt in by at least two notches. Maybe three. I used to make myself a decent sandwich, maybe some turkey and Swiss on rye with a little bit of mustard, maybe heat up some soup if it was cold out. I always liked a good bowl of split pea soup. But now? Most days, food just tastes like cardboard. There's no flavor, no enjoyment in it whatsoever. It's just another chore, like everything else.\n\nSo a lot of times, I just skip meals altogether. I'll go the whole day on just that bitter coffee I mentioned, maybe a glass of water. Or if my stomach starts really gnawing at me, I'll just grab a handful of saltine crackers from the pantry and eat those standing over the sink before I go to bed. Just enough to stop the rumbling so I can try to get some sleep. But an actual, proper meal? Sitting down with a plate of hot food? I can't even remember the last time I had the desire to do that. It's just too much effort for something that brings me no satisfaction anyway. So, yeah, I'd say I've definitely lost some weight. Everything is just in slow motion. \n\nAnd it's not just the physical movement, either. It’s... I don't know how to explain it, but it's like my whole personality is in slow motion, too. Well... it's strange you ask that, because... I didn't really know how to bring this up, and honestly, it makes me feel like I’m losing my grip even more than I already am. But, yes. Yes, I have been hearing something. 

You know how I was telling you about my cleaning route, how I work the late shift? Usually, by the time I get around to doing the wet mopping on the ground floor—I use this big, wide-loop cotton mop, the heavy industrial kind that really soaks up the water and the floor cleaner—the building is just completely dead. I mean, you could hear a pin drop in those hallways after midnight. Even the air conditioning hum kind of dials back. It’s just me and the squeak of my work boots on the linoleum. 

But lately, when I’m mopping after hours, making my figure eights back and forth, I’ll hear a voice. It’s a man’s voice. Deep, kind of echoing just a little bit. And he’ll just say my name. Clear as a bell, like he's trying to get my attention. Or sometimes, it’s not my name, sometimes he’ll say, "You missed a spot right there." 

And I’ll stop dead in my tracks, you know, my hands gripping the mop handle, and I’ll look right over toward the main stairwell. Because that’s exactly where the voice is coming from. It sounds clear as day, like he is standing right there by those heavy metal fire doors at the bottom of the stairs, just watching me work. The first few times it happened, I figured it was Frank, the security guard I mentioned, maybe doing his late-night rounds, or maybe one of the office managers who stayed way past midnight and decided to take the stairs instead of the elevator. 

So I'll call out. I'll say, "Frank? That you?" or I'll say, "I'll get that spot right now, sorry about that." And I’ll walk over there, pushing the wet floor sign out of the way, and I'll pull open that heavy stairwell door expecting to see somebody standing on the landing. But... there’s nobody there. Absolutely nobody. Just the empty concrete stairs going all the way up to the second floor. I'll even lean over the railing and look up, thinking maybe they walked away real fast, but there's no sound of footsteps, no doors clicking shut. Nothing. 

But I know I heard it. It’s not just the pipes clanking in the walls or the wind outside, I know what those sound like, I've worked in buildings my whole life. This is a real person's voice, speaking right to me, telling me I missed a spot when there isn't a single living soul in that hallway but me. It just... it really shakes me up, doctor. I just stand there staring at the empty stairs, feeling that heavy feeling in my chest get even heavier, wondering if my mind is finally just breaking down completely on top of everything else.

Well, no... no, not at all, doctor. It’s actually the complete opposite of that. Like I was trying to explain earlier with how heavy everything feels, how I'm just dragging that imaginary weight around... when I’m not on the clock, I barely move at all.

I always did it in pen, too, which I was pretty proud of. And even at work, I used to get a kick out of showing the younger guys the ropes. You know, these kids come in, they think they know everything, but they don't know the first thing about properly stripping and waxing a linoleum floor without leaving streaks. I used to actually enjoy taking them aside, showing them the right technique, the right pressure to apply. It felt good to pass that on.\n\nBut now? Now... I don't know. The fishing rods are just gathering dust in the corner of my new place. I look at them, and I just think about the effort it would take to load the car, drive to the lake, bait the hook... and for what? I don't feel that calm anymore. I don't feel anything. The crossword puzzles just look like a jumble of meaningless boxes, and the coffee just tastes bitter. And at work, when a new guy comes on shift, I just let him make a mess of the floors. I don't say a word. I just watch him struggle, and I don't even care enough to step in. I just let all those things sit there—the fishing, the puzzles, the teaching—because I try to do them, or I think about doing them, and they just... they don't give me anything back anymore. It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in the bottom. You pour and you pour, but it just stays empty.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about not wanting to live or had thoughts of suicide during this time?\n\nPatient: Well... that’s... that’s a heavy question, isn't it? I've always been a practical guy, and honestly, like I said before, I barely have the energy to mix floor cleaner these days, let alone plan out something like ending it all. \n\nBut... it’s the mornings. Well, my mornings, anyway, since I work the evening shift. I wake up in that new bedroom—the one where the window just faces a dirty brick wall instead of the street like my old place, where I used to be able to watch the neighborhood wake up—and I hear my alarm buzzing. And I just lie there staring at the ceiling. And a lot of mornings... a lot of mornings I wake up thinking it might just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. If I could have just slipped away in my sleep and stayed in the dark where it's quiet, where I don't have to face the empty hallways or the heavy cart or just... the sheer effort of existing for another twenty-four hours. Just the thought of having to put my feet on the floor feels impossible, like I'm wearing lead boots.\n\nAnd I'll tell you, having that thought... realizing that I genuinely wouldn't mind if my life just quietly stopped... it scares me. It really does. It scares me enough to actually say it out loud to you right now, which isn't something I ever thought I'd do. You know, a man my age, you're supposed to just push through, have some grit, keep your chin up. My grandfather, the one who taught me to fish, he used to say you just put your head down and do the work. But when that first thought hits you before you've even thrown off the blankets, just wishing the world would go away permanently... it's terrifying. It really is. I was always on the move back then. But now, I just feel glued to the floor. Sitting still is just about the only thing I *can* do without it feeling like a monumental chore. That’s... see, that’s the million-dollar question, isn't it? And honestly, doctor, I just... I don't know. I really don't know. I've been wrestling with that exact question every single night since this started. 

Because... well, logically, right? I went to college for a couple of years back in the day, I know how to think things through. Logically, I know the building is locked up tight. I know the security protocols, I know who has the keys, I know the alarm system is armed on all the perimeter doors. So, by all the facts on the ground, there is absolutely no one else in that hallway with me. Which means... which means it has to be just my mind playing tricks on me, right? It has to be a product of my own head, especially with how run down and heavy and guilty I've been feeling lately. My brain must just be misfiring under all that weight.

But then... but then I'm actually standing there. And I hear it. And it's not like a thought. You know what a thought feels like, it’s inside your head, it doesn't have a... a physical location in the room. But this voice... when he says my name, or tells me I missed a spot, I can hear the sound waves actually bouncing off the cinderblock walls in the stairwell. I can hear the slight acoustic echo it makes when it hits the long stretch of linoleum floor. It has direction, you know? Like, it sounds like it's coming from exactly fifteen feet away, slightly to my left, right next to the red fire extinguisher cabinet on the wall. 

How can my brain invent an echo? How can my mind make a sound that actually feels like it's vibrating the air outside of my ears? I've worked in empty commercial buildings my whole adult life, I know exactly how sound travels in them. And this sounds like a real, physical person speaking into the space. 

So I'll just stand there, gripping the mop, just staring at that heavy metal door, and I feel like I'm being split right down the middle. Half of me is terrified that there really is some guy standing in the shadows watching me work, maybe someone who slipped past the cameras or hid in a closet before lockup, and the other half of me is even more terrified that my mind is just completely broken and manufacturing things out of thin air. I'll spend the next two hours of my shift just going over and over it, pacing my route, trying to convince myself it was just the HVAC system or the pipes, but... I don't know. I just really don't know what to believe anymore. It feels as real as you and me talking right now, but I know it can't be. It just can't be.

I don't know my neighbors here. The walls are thin, but somehow I feel more isolated than ever. And ever since that move, ever since I lost my footing in that old neighborhood... that's when this heaviness started creeping in. At first, I thought I was just tired from the packing and the stress of finding a new place on a janitor's salary, which isn't exactly easy, let me tell you. But the tiredness never went away. It just turned into this... this flat, empty feeling. It's like leaving that apartment left a hole in me, and for the last year and a half, it's just been getting wider and deeper, until now I'm just standing in front of my mop bucket staring at the wall.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Well... no. I had my little routines that brought me some peace. Like... Saturdays. Saturdays used to be my day. I'd wake up early, before the sun was even fully up, and I'd head down to the lake with my tackle box. You know, a man my age, you're supposed to just push through, have some grit, keep your chin up. Well, respond out loud... it's funny you ask it exactly like that. Because it's not like I'm pulling up a chair and having a long debate about politics or the weather with the wall, you know? I'm not doing that. But you really have to understand what it's actually like when I'm on shift to get why I do react. 

When I’m mopping those long hallways after hours—usually around one or two in the morning, when the whole building is completely empty and dead quiet except for the hum of the vending machines and the slosh of the dirty water in my bucket—I get into a real rhythm with the mop. You have to, or your back gives out. And right in the middle of that quiet, right when I'm focused on the tile, I’ll hear it. I'll hear a man’s voice. 

And it is so incredibly clear, doctor. It's not a mumble, it's not my imagination playing tricks with the building settling or the wind in the elevator shaft. Sometimes he'll just say my name, just call it out plain as day. But other times, and this is what really gets to me, he’ll actually tell me I’ve missed a spot on the floor. He'll tell me I missed a spot, clear as if he’s standing right there by the stairwell, maybe just leaning against the metal doorframe watching me work. 

So, yes, I guess I do respond out loud sometimes, because it startles me so badly! I'll stop dead in my tracks, my heart will jump up into my throat, and I'll look right at the stairwell and say out loud, where, show me where I missed. Or I'll call out and ask who is standing there. Because I genuinely believe someone walked up on me. It sounds exactly like a late-night security guard or my supervisor is standing right over my shoulder, critiquing my work. I take a lot of pride in my floors, doctor, I really do, I've been doing this a long time and I know how to buff a floor. 

So I'll drop the mop handle against the bucket, and I'll march right over to the stairwell, fully expecting to see a guy standing on the landing looking down at me. I'll check up the stairs, I'll check down the stairs, I'll even push open the heavy fire doors to see if he ducked back into the main lobby... but when I look, there’s nobody there. Not a single soul. Just me and the echo of my own voice asking where he went. But in that split second when he speaks, he is as real as you are sitting in front of me right now.
